name: Cheeses Thrice Pizza
subtitle: Holy, profane, and extremely responsive to how the room is doing.
description:
The name is a pun with a congregation and the spokesman is a figure called Jesus Crust who appears on the boxes with his arms out, and Woolbinkle has been asked to modify this by three separate parish committees and has, each time, agreed enthusiastically and changed nothing.

The room reads the room. That is the whole of the phenomenon and it takes about four minutes to become undeniable: when the table by the window laughed, the lights came up a quarter and the far wall came in three feet and the place got cosier; when the couple at the back stopped speaking to each other, the temperature dropped and the ceiling went away somewhere and everybody found themselves sitting further apart.

Nobody adjusts anything. There is no thermostat behind the counter. There is a bull antelope with crooked antlers and thick wool-like fur, watching the door with an expression of enormous and effortful hope.
revisit:
Your order is already in the oven. Woolbinkle says, in the tone of a man laying something down very carefully on a surface he is not sure will hold it, that he had a feeling about four minutes ago and acted on it, and that there is no obligation, and that if he was wrong he would have eaten it himself.

The room is warm in the way only a room with a stone oven in it gets warm — from the floor up, unevenly, better near the back. Chuckles is on in twenty minutes. There are two new cans at the near end of the shelf behind the counter, and the labels are in a hand that has been getting steadier over the fortnight you have been coming here.

lucid.2: The oven is not making the noise the oven is making.
lucid.3: When the room contracts, it contracts by whole feet, in one movement, between one glance and the next. Rooms do not have a smallest unit. This one does.
lucid.4: The room is not responding to the diners' mood. The room and the diners' mood are both being set, from outside, by somebody who is finding the tone difficult tonight.

ambient: Chuckles the Unfunny Clown delivers a joke to the family by the door. It has a structure, and the structure is sound, and the timing is correct, and it does not work — and the family are kind about it in the specific way of people who have been kind about this before.

Somebody laughs politely two tables away, a beat and a half after the moment for it has passed, and a patch of static in the air over the third table thins out and is not there any more. Nobody looks up. Nobody looks at the person who laughed.

The wall decorations are a set of framed harbour prints. At the next table a woman is describing the one nearest her to her companion, in detail, with obvious pleasure, and what she is describing is a pike — a fish, in a cabinet, with a brass plate under it — and her companion agrees that it is a very fine one.
The oven door comes open and the heat arrives at the far wall about two seconds later, and for those two seconds the room is a slightly different shape than it was.
Woolbinkle checks the shelf behind him without turning round, using the reflection in the oven's steel front, and goes back to the peel.

objects.name: the three-cheese blend
objects.description:
The holy secret and the reason the parish committees keep coming. Three cheeses, and Woolbinkle will not say which, and the blend does something in the last forty seconds of the bake that has made this establishment famous in a town that is difficult to make famous anything in.

It patterns. As it goes molten it draws — briefly, legibly, and unmistakably about the person who ordered it. The couple at the back got a closed door. The family by the window got a long table with too many chairs. It resolves into ordinary bubbling within about four seconds and there is a general understanding in Silvora Reefs that you do not comment on somebody else's.

Yours is coming out now. Woolbinkle is standing between you and the oven with a peel in his hands and his shoulders set.
objects.repeat: He stands in front of the oven every time now. He has started doing it before you ask, and he does it apologetically, with his back to the heat and his hands where you can see them, like a man guarding something he does not think he has the right to guard.
objects.monocle: Through the gold you do not need him to move. The pattern is legible through him: it is a page, and it is dense, and it has a wide left margin and a ragged right one, and about two thirds of the way down there is a gap where a paragraph has been taken out and the surrounding text has not been closed up.

check.prompt: Get him to move. He is a bull antelope with a peel and a great deal of anxiety and he is standing between you and the only oven in this parish that anybody talks about, and he is not going to be moved by asking.
check.success:
You do not ask him to move. You ask him what he got, when he orders one for himself, at the end of a shift, alone.

He puts the peel down.

"A can," he says. "Every time. Been a can for eleven years." And he steps aside — not to show you yours, but because a man who has just said that is not standing anywhere on purpose any more.

Yours is on the stone. It is a page. Dense type, wide left margin, ragged right, and two thirds of the way down a gap where something has been taken out and the text around it has not been closed up. It holds for four seconds and it is not a symbol and it is not a metaphor and you have read enough of it to know the rhythm of the sentences.

Then it is cheese, and it is very good, and Woolbinkle says, quietly, "Your thoughts are particularly spicy today," which is what he says, and which he has clearly been saying for years to avoid saying anything else.
check.failure: He does not move. He is enormous and gentle and completely immovable and he talks the entire four seconds — about the blend, about the oven, about the parish committee and the third letter from the parish committee — and by the end of it the pattern has resolved and the pizza is a pizza and he is holding it out to you with both hands and an expression of hope so undefended that pressing further would be a kind of assault.

clue.title: A page with a paragraph removed
clue.text: Oliver's cheese patterns into a dense page — wide left margin, ragged right — with a gap two thirds down where a paragraph has been removed and the surrounding text not closed up.

objects.name: the patches of silence
objects.description:
Chuckles is not funny. That is not an opinion held about Chuckles by the room; it is his professional situation, established over six years, and he has been in it a long time and continues to arrive on time and set up his own microphone.

When a joke fails in this building, the failure has a physical consequence.

A patch of air about a yard across goes thick. Sometimes it is a fog, low and slow-moving. Sometimes it is a kind of dry static that makes the light behind it grainy and takes the edge off anything seen through it. And it stays exactly where it happened, at head height, in the middle of a working restaurant.

Diners walk around them without appearing to notice they are doing it. There are four in the room at the moment. Two of them are old enough to have collected an ashtray and a folded napkin, which have been placed there deliberately, by somebody who knows the patch is not going anywhere.

A polite laugh dissolves them. Anybody's. It does not have to be sincere, it does not have to be loud, and it does not have to come from anywhere near the patch.
objects.repeat: Six now. The new ones are by the counter, which means he has been working closer to the door than he likes, which means the tables further in were occupied and he took the harder pitch rather than wait.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the patches are not fog. They are blank. Not white — *unwritten*, with the texture of paper that has had nothing put on it, and the room's description simply stops at the edge of each one and resumes on the other side.

passive.text: A polite laugh dissolves them and sincerity is not required. That means the mechanism is not responding to feeling. It is responding to the *sound being made*, which is a much shorter chain of causation and a much worse one.

He knows. Watch him after one lands wrong: he does not look at the audience, he looks at the air, to see how big it is. He has been measuring his own failures by the yard for years and he keeps coming back, and the reason he keeps coming back is that he is the only one who can clear them.

clue.title: Silence that takes up room
clue.text: Failed jokes at Cheeses Thrice leave physical yard-wide patches of thickened air that any polite laugh — sincere or not — dissolves. Sound, not feeling, is the mechanism.

clue.title: Unwritten, not white
clue.text: Under the monocle the silence-patches are blank paper. The room's description stops at the edge of each and resumes on the far side.

check.prompt: The fog off the harbour comes up this street and stops at the door of every other establishment on it. Stand in the doorway and work out what this one is doing that the others are not.
check.success:
It is not cold and it is not wet and it has a direction that has nothing to do with the wind.

It is coming *from* the far end of the parish rather than from the sea, and there is a pressure in it like the pressure at the edge of a held note, and four streets over somebody stops what they are doing at the same moment you do.
check.failure:
Fog. It comes up the street off the harbour, goes over you and past you and on toward the lamps, and it is — as far as any part of you can establish, standing in a doorway in the cold with an oven behind you — weather.

The patch over the third table does not care that you are looking at it. It is a yard of thickened air in a restaurant, it has been there since before you came in, and it declines absolutely to be anything more interesting than that while a man is standing in the doorway waiting for it to be.

clue.title: The fog comes from the far end
clue.text: The fog does not come off the sea. It comes from the far end of the parish, carrying a pressure like the edge of a held note.

objects.name: the wall decorations
objects.description:
Framed harbour prints. Six of them in a row above the banquette, matted and glazed and hung dead level: the breakwater, the fish quay, two of the lighthouse taken in different years, one of the boats laid up for winter, and a long one of the whole waterfront in weather.

They are unremarkable. That is the point of them; they are the sort of thing a franchise sends out by the crate to make a room look furnished.

The couple at the next table have been in this room as long as you have. Ask them — and you have — and they will tell you without hesitating, without any sense that they are contradicting anybody, and with the mild puzzlement of people being asked to confirm the obvious, that the wall above the banquette has a mounted pike on it. A fish. In a case, with a brass plate. And always has.

You can both point at it. You have done, twice. Your fingers arrive at the same place on the same wall, at the same height, and neither of you is being difficult, and neither of you is wrong.
objects.repeat: Still prints for you. The couple who were describing a pike have gone and been replaced by a man on his own who is looking at the same frame and seeing, going by his expression, neither a print nor a pike.
objects.monocle: Through the gold there is nothing above the banquette. Not a blank wall — a blank *space*, with the same unwritten texture as Chuckles' fog, and a note in the margin beside it in small pencil: SOMETHING ON THIS WALL.

passive.text: Neither of you is wrong and neither of you is going to give way, and the striking thing is that neither of you finds the disagreement interesting. The not-finding-it-interesting is the load-bearing part.
Six prints. The pike is one object. Whatever is on that wall, everybody gets the right number of *hooks* — the nail positions are the fixed thing and the contents are not.

clue.title: The nails are fixed. The contents are not.
clue.text: Two diners describe entirely different decorations above the same banquette and point at the same place. The nail positions are constant; what hangs on them is not.

clue.title: SOMETHING ON THIS WALL
clue.text: Under the monocle the banquette wall is blank in the unwritten sense, with a pencil note in the margin beside it reading SOMETHING ON THIS WALL.

check.prompt: Franchise decor, mass-produced, identical to a thousand other rooms — except that no two people in this room have ever agreed about what is on that wall. Look at the frames rather than the pictures.
check.success:
Eleven framed prints, all of them stock, all of them the same three photographs in rotation — and the ninth is not a print.

It is a photograph of this room, taken from where you are standing, with the prints on the wall in it, and in that photograph the ninth frame contains a photograph of this room.
check.failure:
Eleven frames of exactly the kind of nothing they are meant to be. The breakwater. The fish quay. The lighthouse twice. A smell of oregano over everything and a warm draught off the oven every time the door comes open.

And a bull antelope watching you look at his wall with the patience of somebody who is entirely used to it — who has watched a great many people look at this wall and has never once asked any of them what they were seeing, because he has worked out that the asking is the part that upsets people.

clue.title: The ninth frame
clue.text: One frame at Cheeses Thrice holds a photograph of the room it hangs in, containing itself, taken from where a customer stands.

objects.name: the shelf of cans
objects.description:
Behind the counter, at head height, running the whole length of the wall: cans.

Not stock. Stock is in the back and you have seen the back — sacks and tins and a chest freezer, ordinary and well kept. These are on display, on a shelf that was built for them, at a height where they can be reached without a stool and read without leaning.

They are labelled in Woolbinkle's own hand, and they are not food.

The labels are dates and single words. *March, patience.* *Two winters ago, the letter.* *A Tuesday, hope, unopened.* *The night of the thing with the van.* Forty or so of them, going back years, arranged in an order that is not chronological and not alphabetical and is clearly an order.

The newest four are at the near end and they are dusty in a way that says they were put up together, at the same time, some while ago — and that nothing has been added since.

He has told you, when asked directly, that he cans things. He said it the way a man says that he swims.
objects.repeat: There is a new one at the near end. It says: *Tonight, the man who asked.* The hand is unsteady in the way of somebody writing something down before they can talk themselves out of it.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the cans are exactly what the labels say, sealed and airtight and completely intact, and every one of them is holding. It is the only shelf of anything in Silvora Reefs that is not leaking, revising, or quietly disagreeing with itself, and it has been built by hand out of the only technique its maker had.

passive.text: This is not a hobby and it is not a symptom. A creature who was once unable to keep something has worked out a method and has been applying it, carefully, every time, for years. It is the most functional thing in this town.

Can, can't, can-can, cannibal, cantaloupe, can't elope. The whole tangle is one verb doing four jobs, and the joke everybody in Silvora Reefs tells at his expense is a joke about a creature who could not do a thing — and he has spent eleven years demonstrating, on a shelf, in public, that he *can*.

clue.title: Forty cans, all holding
clue.text: Woolbinkle's shelf holds forty hand-labelled cans of things that are not food — 'March, patience', 'A Tuesday, hope, unopened' — and every one of them is sealed and intact.

check.prompt: He will not tell you what is in the cans and he will not lie to you about it either, which leaves exactly one route. Arrange for him to want to tell you.
check.success:
You stop asking about the cans and start being interested in the *sealing*, which is a craft, and which nobody has asked him about in eleven years.

He talks for a quarter of an hour about pressure and headspace, and somewhere in the middle of it he says, without noticing he is saying it, that the difficult ones are the ones that are still going on when you seal them — and then he stops, and looks at the shelf, and does not take it back.
check.failure: You come at it from the side and he watches you come, pleasantly, the whole way. "You want to know what's in them," he says, not unkindly, and puts a slice in front of you, and that is the end of the subject for tonight.

clue.title: The ones still going on
clue.text: Woolbinkle lets slip that the difficult cans are the ones still going on when they are sealed — then stops, and looks at the shelf, and does not retract it.

objects.name: the poem on the wall
objects.description:
Framed, behind the till, at a height that suggests it was hung by somebody who did not want to be observed hanging it and did not want it read too easily afterwards.

THE CAN'T ELOPE ANTELOPE. Forty-odd lines of the most relentless punning in the parish — the cans and the can'ts and the can-can, the belle who would not fool with a full-of-bull fool of a bull antelope — and it is genuinely, properly funny. It is funny in the first line and it is still funny in the fortieth, which is very much harder than it looks and does not happen by accident.

The frame is good. The glass has been cleaned recently and cleaned well, on both sides, which means somebody took it off the wall to do it.

Woolbinkle hung it himself. He has never mentioned it, and he has never once been in the room when anybody has read it aloud, and the poem is in three establishments in this town and this is the only one where the antelope put it up.
objects.repeat: Still behind the till, still hung slightly too high to read comfortably, which you have stopped believing is an accident. The glass has been cleaned again since Tuesday, on both sides.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the poem is a draft with the corrections still showing, and every correction moves in the same direction, which is toward mercy.

passive.text: Forty lines and not one of them takes a free shot. Every joke here is at the expense of the *language* and not one of them is at the expense of the antelope, which given the subject matter is a considerable piece of engineering.

clue.title: He hung it himself
clue.text: The Can't Elope Antelope hangs behind the till at Cheeses Thrice, put up by Woolbinkle, who has never mentioned it. It is the only one of the three copies in the parish that the antelope hung.

check.prompt: Everybody in this parish knows what the poem is about, and knowing that is what stops them reading it. Read it as a composition instead — for what it is *doing* rather than who it is about.
check.success:
It is not about an antelope.

Structurally it is four movements and every one of them turns on a refusal, and the refusals soften as the poem goes: the first is a slammed door, the second is an argument, the third is a hesitation dressed as a joke, and the fourth is barely a no at all.

A poem that wanted to condemn him would run that sequence the other way round. This one is built — carefully, over forty lines, by somebody with a great deal of technique — to arrive at a place where the thing he did is *survivable*.

And the meter breaks in exactly one place. One. In a poem this tight that is not a slip, it is a signature, and it breaks on the word *nope*.
check.failure: You read it four times and it is four times funny, which is its defence and has always been its defence. The technique closes over the subject like water over a stone and will not let you get at what is underneath it tonight.

clue.title: The poem is a defence
clue.text: Read as composition, the Can't Elope Antelope softens its refusals across four movements — engineered to arrive somewhere the antelope's worst act is survivable. The meter breaks exactly once, on the word 'nope'.

objects.name: the room, when Chuckles is on
objects.description:
Eleven tables, a low stage that is really a pallet with a cloth over it, and a man in a checked jacket doing material that is not going to work.

It does not work. The room knows within about four words that it is not going to work — there is a particular quality to the quiet that arrives when a joke has been recognised as a joke and declined — and the comedian knows it too, and carries on, because carrying on is the job.

What the room does next is the thing worth watching.

Nothing visible happens. Nobody catches anybody's eye. Nobody nudges anybody. And then, from table nine, a beat and a half late and entirely alone, somebody laughs — not the laugh of a person who found it funny, but a clear, deliberate, carrying laugh, produced on purpose, at some social cost, by a person eating on their own.

And then table four does it. And then the pair by the window.
objects.repeat: He is on again. The room is doing it again — late, scattered, unsignalled — and it is doing it without any of them having agreed to, and the patch over the third table is thinning while you watch.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the room is not an audience. It is a repair crew, and it is working, and the patch it is closing is above the third table and about a yard across.

passive.text: Somebody laughs about a beat and a half late, from three tables off, alone, on purpose. And then somebody else does. They are not laughing at the joke and they are not laughing at him.

clue.title: The room repairs him
clue.text: When a joke dies at Cheeses Thrice, laughter arrives late, deliberately, from scattered tables — from people who are not laughing at the joke and not laughing at the comedian.

check.prompt: Something in this room is being organised without anybody organising it, eleven times a night, six nights a week. Stop watching the stage and listen for the whole parish at once.
check.success:
Nobody signals. That is the finding and it takes a moment to be sure of, because the coordination is so good that a signal is the natural assumption.

The laugh comes from table nine, late and solitary. Table four joins it. Then the pair by the window, then a man on his own by the oven who does not look up from his plate while doing it — and the patch of thickened air over the third table thins out and goes, and the comedian gets to the end of his set believing he has died, which he has, and the room lets him believe it because the alternative is telling him what he is for.

Eleven times a night. Six years. Nobody has ever mentioned it to anybody, including each other.
check.failure:
A bad set in a warm room, and some laughter, and some not, and a comedian working through it with the dogged competence of a man who has died in better rooms than this.

The kindness in here is real. It is going on right now, four feet from where you are standing. And it is not going to be caught in the act by a man at the back of the room who has decided to watch for it — because the whole mechanism depends on nobody in here believing they are part of a mechanism.

clue.title: Nobody signals
clue.text: The late scattered laughter that clears the thickened air at Cheeses Thrice is completely uncoordinated — no signal, no glance, eleven times a night for six years, and nobody has ever mentioned it to anybody, including each other.
